author: Matt Jaworowski
title: Giant snapping turtle rescued on Lake Michigan beach - NewsBreak
text:
By Matt Jaworowski No media credit provided. ,
9 hours ago GRAND HAVEN, Mich. (WOOD) — A giant snapping turtle is going viral across West Michigan after he was brought to a local sanctuary last week.
The Michigan Amphibian & Reptile Sanctuary says its volunteers took in a 33-pound snapping turtle last Friday after he was found on the beach in Grand Haven.
“At roughly 33 pounds of pure turtle, he is an absolute tank, and my goodness is he pretty!” the sanctuary said in a social media post .
Snapping turtles are rarely found along Lake Michigan because the heavy waves are not an ideal habitat for them. Even the giant turtle was struggling in the waves when he was found on Friday.
“(A volunteer found him) being tumbled around by the waves, and she said he had no fight left in him when she reached him,” the post read.
The turtle, now named Doug, was transported to the Paw Paw Veterinary Clinic to undergo several tests. He will be monitored for at least the next month.
Doug the Tank, a 33-pound snapping turtle, was rescued last week on a Lake Michigan Beach in Grand Haven. (Courtesy Michigan Amphibian & Reptile Sanctuary) Doug the Tank, a 33-pound snapping turtle, was rescued last week on a Lake Michigan Beach in Grand Haven. (Courtesy Michigan Amphibian & Reptile Sanctuary) Doug the Tank, a 33-pound snapping turtle, was rescued last week on a Lake Michigan Beach in Grand Haven. (Courtesy Michigan Amphibian & Reptile Sanctuary) “Despite the sass in the photos, he’s exhausted and extremely worn down, but we are anticipating a swift recovery,” the post said.
The sanctuary hypothesized that someone may have helped Doug cross a nearby roadway, thinking he was trying to get to Lake Michigan.
“Unfortunately, this type of relocation can displace wildlife into habitats that are completely unsuitable for them, which can quickly become life-threatening,” the post said. “With this guy likely being at least in his mid to late 30’s, I have to imagine it would be quite upsetting to spend over 30 years getting to know your home range like the back of your hand, only to be ripped away and dropped off in a completely new and uninhabitable location.”
The Michigan Amphibian & Reptile Sanctuary is a 501c nonprofit organization specifically licensed for wildlife rehabilitation. The sanctuary’s post has gotten more than 5,000 reactions on Facebook. MARS Executive Director Kayla Yarbrough told News 8 they are sharing Doug’s story to encourage more donations.
“We can only do what we do for the animals thanks to the gracious support of our donors,” Yarbrough said. “We are always happy to help our reptile and amphibian neighbors, so if anyone encounters an injured or struggling animal, please don’t hesitate to reach out to us.”
